seo.title: Karmic tail 9 21 21 compatibility: The Hermit and two Worlds
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 21 21 compatibility: two people become each other's shelter, then a whole world, and their main task is the wider world. Read through John Donne.

title: Couple's karmic tail 9-21-21: how two people become each other's hermitage and a whole world
short: The Hermit at the entry and The World twice over — an odd set for two people: one card about solitude, two about the whole wide world. In the couple's tail 9-21-21 this is not a contradiction but a plot. First the two become each other's shelter, then a whole world for two, and the main task turns out to be the big world: friends, roads, change, other people's eyes.

sections.h2: The stanza that holds the whole tail
paragraphs: Donne's "The Canonization" is a poem about two people whom the world condemns for their love. The poet's answer: one day they will be made saints, and the lovers of the future will pray to them. The last stanza is that prayer (spelling modernised from Grierson's 1912 edition):

And thus invoke us: "You whom reverend love / Made one another's hermitage; / You, to whom love was peace, that now is rage; / Who did the whole world's soul contract, and drove / Into the glasses of your eyes / (So made such mirrors, and such spies, / That they did all to you epitomize) / Countries, towns, courts: beg from above / A pattern of your love!"
The stanza moves in three steps, in the order of the tail 9-21-21.

First comes "one another's hermitage". A hermitage is a hermit's dwelling, a cell in the wilderness where people went to leave the world; Russian has an exact word for it, pustyn. Love made the two a hermitage **for each other**: they did not retreat to a cell — each became a cell for the other. This is The Hermit at the entry.

Then comes the whole world, shrunk to the size of a pupil. Countries, towns and royal courts fit into the eyes of two people: they learn the world through each other and need nothing more. This is The World in the middle: the couple lives inside a universe of its own.

And finally come those who arrive later, with a request for a pattern. The world again, but someone else's now: people beyond the threshold who might gain something from this love. This is the main task — a World that is not inside the pupil but out there.

In Russian the stanza gains an extra layer: the word mir means both "peace" and "world", so "love was peace" reads at once as calm and as a universe. And the word hermitage has a Russian destiny everyone knows: the Hermitage in St Petersburg. Catherine the Great conceived it as a cosy private retreat for herself, and it grew into a museum filled with art from all over the world. A hermitage that holds a world is not just a figure of speech.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: "For God's sake hold your tongue, and let me love"
paragraphs: "The Canonization" begins not with a prayer but with a shout: "For God's sake hold your tongue, and let me love." The poet goes on to list what the uninvited adviser could do instead: grow rich, study, seek a post, court the great, gaze at the King's face — the real one or the one stamped on a coin. Anything, as long as he lets them love. "Alas, alas, who's injured by my love?" Soldiers still find wars and lawyers still find litigious men, "though she and I do love."

This is how The Hermit sounds at the entry to the couple's tail. The wish is shared: to be left alone. Not out of hostility to people, but because, together, it is finally quiet. In daily life it looks ordinary. Friends hear about the engagement after the rings are bought. The third invitation of the month is politely declined, and both are glad. A conversation that started at dinner ends at three in the morning. Each has a corner and a time of their own, and the other does not barge in. Love is shown in deeds: a fixed tap, a scarf that somehow ended up in the bag, knowing when to fall silent. Every step is taken slowly — from the first kiss to a shared key.
The light in such a hermitage is their own, and they pay for it themselves. Donne has a line for this: "We're tapers too, and at our own cost die."

But the entry point stands on the line of tasks, and Lisovskaya warns that the same wish can turn into resistance. Donne knew this shadow too — in another poem, "The Good-Morrow". The lovers ask themselves what they did before love: "Or snorted we in the seven sleepers' den?" In the old legend, seven young men of Ephesus hid in a cave from persecution and slept there for centuries. When one of them went down to the town for bread, his coins gave him away: they had been struck under a long-dead emperor. The hiding place worked too well. The world moved on, and they were left with money in their pockets that nobody would take. In Donne the cave is life before love, but the image also fits what the hermitage itself can become.

This is the entry on the minus side: a hermitage where the two do not withdraw but hide. Problems pile up in silence, because any hard conversation would break the quiet. Each sits in a shell and calls it respect for boundaries. Being together feels uncomfortable at times, but stepping outside is more frightening.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: one little room becomes an everywhere
paragraphs: In the same "The Good-Morrow" the two wake up from the cave and look at each other:

And now good morrow to our waking souls, / Which watch not one another out of fear; / For love, all love of other sights controls, / And makes one little room an everywhere. / Let sea-discoverers to new worlds have gone, / Let maps to other, worlds on worlds have shown, / Let us possess one world, each hath one, and is one.

Donne lived in the age of the first atlases, when ships came back from the New World with new coastlines for the maps. He answers a whole era: we have no need to sail, everything is here. **One little room becomes an everywhere** — that is The World in the middle of the task, how the couple lives the path from the wish for quiet to the main task.

In life, the room turns into a universe gradually. The two develop a language of their own: pet words, nicknames, jokes there is no one to explain to. Their philosophy — how to spend, how to rest, what to believe — fits so well that there is almost nothing to argue about. Chores are split down the middle. Each accepts the other whole, even on bad days. Often The World is literal: the couple moves to another city or another country, lives between two addresses or through work trips, and misses each other more after every separation.

Next Donne offers an image that maps exactly onto the numbers: "My face in thine eye, thine in mine appears… Where can we find two better hemispheres, / Without sharp north, without declining west?" Two faces in two pupils — two hemispheres of one globe. The tail says the same: The World plus The World, 21 + 21 = 42, which reduces to 6. The Lovers. They stand in the centre of the chart for every single couple with the tail 9-21-21.

The line "each hath one, and is one" is about two universes, not one. The couple holds together as long as it remembers this: its world is made of two wholes, not two halves. Donne adds a formula of the old philosophers: "Whatever dies, was not mixed equally." Mixed equally means that neither has dissolved in the other.

The middle has an oddity that only shows up in the calculation. A personal chart never has such a middle: by the personal tail formula, The Empress would stand between The Hermit and The World — house, garden, household (9 + 21 = 30 → 3). The couple has The World in that place. The two walk the path not through a house but through a universe — through something neither of them has alone.

sections.h2: Main task: "She is all states, and all princes, I; nothing else is"
paragraphs: The main point of the tail is the third, and it is read mainly through the minus: what the couple does not manage and what it needs to learn. For 9-21-21 Donne has a warning poem, funny and arrogant. It is called "The Sun Rising".

The lovers chase away the sun that has looked in at the window: "Busy old fool, unruly Sun, / Why dost thou thus, / Through windows, and through curtains call on us?" Let it go and wake late schoolboys and the King's huntsmen. "Love, all alike, no season knows, nor clime, / Nor hours, days, months, which are the rags of time." And further: "She is all states, and all princes, I, / Nothing else is." The sun is even offered an easier job: since its duty is to warm the world, let it warm the two of them, because they are the world. "This bed thy centre is, these walls, thy sphere."

This is **The World shrunk to four walls** — the main task on the minus side. In Lisovskaya it stands for very down-to-earth things, and a couple recognises them as scenes. Friends drop away one by one: people stopped inviting them, since they would only say no. One partner's hobby — a choir, football, a pottery class — becomes "not ours", first teased, then mocked. One partner patiently re-educates the other into the shared worldview. Evenings repeat like Groundhog Day, and any novelty, from a holiday to moving the furniture, is met as a threat. Agreement does not come: each pulls the blanket to their own side and does not hear the other. And when the closed world gets cramped, someone slams the door — comes back — and slams it again. Together, apart, together.

"The Sun Rising" argues not only with the sun but with the card itself. Waite gives the old names of The World: "The World, the Universe, or Time." The lovers call time rags, yet this couple has that card twice. Two people who stop the clocks in their room are at war with their own tail. In Waite's divinatory list the same card has a reverse side — "Inertia, fixity, stagnation, permanence" — and Wen writes of a person who "is afraid of change and is hesitating to take the necessary actions."

Donne knew what makes such a fortress dangerous. In "The Anniversary" the lovers are kings whom nothing can threaten: "Who is so safe as we? where none can do / Treason to us, except one of us two." In a world with nobody else in it, the threat can only come from inside. Most often this is not a loud act but a quiet one: one partner has long wanted out and says nothing, because to speak would be to wreck the universe.

Wen compares The World to the Gaia hypothesis, in which the Earth is a living organism, and writes that to fulfil an ultimate purpose a person "must embrace the spiritual dimension of the Seeker's relationship with his or her environment." For the couple this is the main task: its world has to be in a relationship with the shared one — neither under siege nor in exile.

One boundary. If one partner forbids the other friends and family, checks up on them and will not let them go, this is no longer solitude and no longer the card — it is control. That calls for a counsellor or psychologist, and in danger, a local emergency number.

sections.h2: Donne and Anne More: from "Un-done" to "no man is an island"
paragraphs: Donne was not writing from hearsay. In December 1601 the twenty-nine-year-old secretary to Sir Thomas Egerton, Lord Keeper of the Great Seal, secretly married seventeen-year-old Anne More, the niece of his employer's wife. The bride's father had Donne dismissed, and Donne and the friends who arranged the wedding were sent to prison. Donne's first biographer, Izaak Walton, writes that Donne told his wife of his dismissal by letter and added after his signature: "John Donne, Anne Donne, Un-done."

The court and a career — the world in the most literal sense — closed to them. The years that followed were that very hermitage. First Anne's kinsman, Sir Francis Wolley, took them into his house at Pyrford, where, in Walton's words, they lived "with much freedom to themselves". Then came a cramped house at Mitcham near London, full of children and cares, on very little money.

"The Canonization" and "The Sun Rising" are often read as poems about Donne's own marriage. The grounds are indirect: "The Canonization" has "my five gray hairs, or ruined fortune", and both poems have a king — and King James came to the throne in 1603, a year after the poet lost his post. No document dates these poems: they were printed only in 1633, after the author's death.

What does survive is the letters from Mitcham, and Walton quotes them in his Life. "To be no part of any body, is as to be nothing," Donne writes to a friend, and admits he will judge himself nothing unless he can be "incorporated into a part of the world". The man who declared in verse that beyond the two of them "nothing else is" was, in prose, homesick for the big world. This is the main task of 9-21-21, spoken by the hero himself: a hermitage for two does not cancel the need to be part of a whole.

Walton also describes how the family lived in those years. Wife and children stayed at Mitcham, while Donne took lodgings in London near Whitehall, where friends and business drew him, and often went back — to his family and his books: "to that place and such studies, he could willingly have wedded himself during his life." One leg stands, the other walks. This is no longer a closed room but a pair of compasses.

In 1624 Donne would write a sentence that people know even when they do not know the author: "No man is an island, entire of itself; every man is a piece of the continent, a part of the main." Hemingway took it as the epigraph for "For Whom the Bell Tolls". The road from "nothing else is" to "no man is an island" is the road of the tail 9-21-21 from its middle to its main task.

sections.h2: The compasses: a circle drawn by spreading the legs
paragraphs: Donne's most famous love poem is "A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning". Walton says it was "a copy of verses given by Mr. Donne to his wife at the time he then parted from her", when he left for France with his patron Sir Robert Drury — that was 1611. Anne did not want to let him go and, in Walton's phrase, consented "with an unwilling-willingness".
The poem opens with The Hermit's silence: "So let us melt, and make no noise… 'Twere profanation of our joys / To tell the laity our love." And it ends with a circle:

If they be two, they are two so / As stiff twin compasses are two; / Thy soul, the fixed foot, makes no show / To move, but doth, if the other do. / And though it in the centre sit, / Yet when the other far doth roam, / It leans and hearkens after it, / And grows erect, as that comes home. / Such wilt thou be to me, who must, / Like th' other foot, obliquely run; / Thy firmness makes my circle just, / And makes me end where I begun.

Here is the answer to the main task of 9-21-21. The World is no longer a room or a bed as "centre". It is **a circle that can only be drawn by spreading the legs**. Pressed together, they put a dot on the paper. The circle appears when one leg goes far and the other holds the centre, and the two are joined so that one listens for the other. A leg that runs off without a centre draws not a circle but a line: that is the together-apart pattern.

In Waite, both legs are written into one card. The upright divinatory list of The World reads "voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place"; the reversed list, "fixity… permanence". Taken apart, they mean flight or paralysis. Taken together, they make a pair of compasses: one leg walks, the other stands, and a circle comes out. This is our reading, not Waite's, but it fits a tail in which The World stands twice.

The last line also matches the numbers. "And makes me end where I begun": the main task plus the centre lead back to the entry. 21 + 6 = 27 → 9 — The World plus The Lovers give The Hermit. The couple's circle closes on the very hermitage it began with, only now they return to it rather than hide in it.

In Donne the fixed foot is the wife and the roaming one is himself: that was how things were arranged in 1611. The couple's tail does not care about sex. Either partner can hold the centre or go far, and a strong 9-21-21 couple swaps legs: today one packs for the road, tomorrow the other.

Donne describes parting in words worth remembering: "Our two souls therefore, which are one, / Though I must go, endure not yet / A breach, but an expansion, / Like gold to airy thinness beat." **Not a breach, but an expansion** — that is what the main task teaches the couple.

"The couple's values" matter here as well — the point that answers why the two are together and which path they should take. In couples with the tail 9-21-21 two cards share it almost equally: The Hermit in 51.1% and The Moon in 48.9%.

ul: **If The Hermit is in the values**, the hermitage stands twice — at the entry and at the very heart. For such a couple solitude is not a concession but a value. The task is not to give it up but to make sure each partner also has solitude of their own, so that the shared kind does not become a cage.

**If The Moon is in the values**, a line from the same "Valediction" comes to mind: "Dull sublunary lovers' love / (Whose soul is sense) cannot admit / Absence." Donne is teasing, but he is precise: to the old cosmographers the sublunary world was the world of change, where everything shifts. Wen sees in The Moon "a strong theme of conservation in the card, rather than exploration or expansion", a need to feel protected, "the tough outer shell". Waite writes of "the fears of the natural mind in the presence of that place of exit, when there is only reflected light to guide it." For such a couple one partner's departure stirs up fears and invented stories, and a conversation about the fear before the parting matters more than phone calls during it.

sections.h2: The couple's centre — The Lovers: a pattern, not an icon
paragraphs: Every couple with the tail 9-21-21 has the same centre of the chart, the atmosphere inside the couple: The Lovers, 6. Waite calls the card "The Lovers or Marriage" and writes that in its eighteenth-century form "it is really a card of married life, shewing father and mother, with their child placed between them", and that it "is said to have been entitled Simulacrum fidei, the symbol of conjugal faith". Wen starts elsewhere: "in every traditional interpretation of The Lovers, the card is about a moral choice, about choosing the right path," and only then about romance. And what it means is "partnership with one other person."

For 9-21-21 this means that the air between two worlds is a choice made anew every day. On the plus side it is sincerity, a lot of touch, decisions taken together even in small things, no secrets from each other.

On the minus side The Lovers have traps of their own, and "The Canonization" points straight at one: idealisation. A couple "canonized for love" can no longer be touched: every quarrel looks like sacrilege, every imperfection like betrayal of the pattern. Among the tasks of The Lovers Lisovskaya names perfectionism and idealising the relationship. The pattern asked for in Donne's stanza is alive, not an icon on the wall.

Wen adds one more detail to this arithmetic. For her, The Hermit and The World are both cards of the element of Earth, and in both yin energy is dominant. The Lovers are Air and yang. A quiet, heavy, earthbound tail — and a light centre where a choice is made every day.

sections.h2: Clues in the numbers: what every 9-21-21 couple shares
paragraphs: The tail 9-21-21 occurs in about one couple in 116 (0.864%) — 42nd place among the 97 couple tails. The clues in it are the same for all such couples, whatever their dates.

ul: **Both Worlds are exact sums.** In a couple's chart a number from 13 to 22 can only come from addition without reduction. In these couples the middle always adds up to exactly 21 (4 + 17, 6 + 15, 3 + 18 or 7 + 14), and so does the main task (10 + 11, 15 + 6, 12 + 9 or 13 + 8). The World does not appear "by itself" here; the two assemble it.

**The Hermit at the entry is always 27, reduced to nine.** In almost nine couples out of ten (88%) it is made of The World and The Lovers: one partner has the personal tail 21-4-10, the other 6-17-11, and 21 + 6 give 27. In the rest it is The Moon and The Hermit, 18 + 9: personal tails 18-6-15 and 9-15-6 (10%) or 18-3-12 and 9-18-9 (2%). The very rare pairing 21-7-13 and 6-14-8 again gives The World plus The Lovers. The hermitage for two is made of a world and of love.

**The centre is The Lovers in 100% of such couples.** Lisovskaya advises adding up energies that repeat: if the sum stands in the chart, it sounds in the couple. Two Worlds give 21 + 21 = 42 → 6, and the six is not an echo but the centre. The sum of the whole tail, 9 + 21 + 21 = 51 → 6, is The Lovers again.

**The entry and the centre behave as in a personal chart; the middle does not.** The main task plus the centre give the entry: 21 + 6 = 27 → 9, which is how the entry of a personal tail is always built. But the middle breaks the rule: in a personal chart it would be 9 + 21 → 3. So nobody has 9-21-21 as a personal tail — it is a tail that exists only for two.
**The couple's values are The Hermit (51.1%) or The Moon (48.9%).** Half the couples meet their first card again — where it is decided why they are together.

paragraphs: In passing, Waite is worth recalling: his Hermit "blends the idea of the Ancient of Days with the Light of the World." In the tail 9-21-21 two Worlds stand behind that light, one after the other.

sections.h2: How to calculate the couple's tail 9-21-21: an example
paragraphs: Each point of the couple's chart is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts, reduced to 22. The couple's middle is not recalculated from the two outer numbers: it is added up from the partners' middles.
Take the dates 14.10.1975 and 05.11.1975. The first person's personal tail is 21-4-10, the second's is 6-17-11. Add them point by point:

The couple's tail is 9-21-21. The centre is added up from the personal centres 11 and 13, giving 6. This couple's "values" are 18, The Moon. This is the most common pairing of personal tails, 88% of all 9-21-21 couples.

sections.h2: What changes the script for a 9-21-21 couple
paragraphs: The way out is not to tear down the hermitage but to cut a door into it and learn to draw a circle.

ul: **A door on schedule.** One regular evening with guests, relatives, friends in the house. Not a duty but fresh air: a world that comes into the room stops being a threat.

**A road of one's own for each.** Each partner has something outside the couple — a trip, a circle of people, a project — and the other does not treat it as betrayal. The compasses only work when the legs are apart.
**The legs take turns.** It is not always the same person who goes off. Whoever holds the centre today may leave tomorrow.
**A ritual of return.** "And grows erect, as that comes home": the meeting after a parting matters more than the goodbye. Tell what was seen on the road, and listen to how life went at home.
**The other's world is not a province.** Ask about the partner's hobbies and plans the way one asks about an unfamiliar country, instead of reshaping them to the shared philosophy.

**A check against an outside view.** When the couple's judgements about everyone around grow too unanimous, it helps to ask a friend how it looks from outside. Eyes that act as "spies" do not see everything.
**Finishing things.** The World is the card of completion. A renovation, a trip, a joint project is better finished and celebrated than kept for years in a state of "we'll get to it".
**Talking before the trip.** Especially if The Moon is in the values: speak about the fear of separation before it, not in phone calls during it.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail: a hermitage with an open door
paragraphs: In the strong version of 9-21-21 the hermitage remains a hermitage. The two still feel best together, talk late into the night and have no need of crowds. But the room has become an everywhere not because the world was shut outside, but because it has windows and a door, and people pass through them both ways.

Such couples need no persuading to become a pattern. People come to them on their own — to sit in the kitchen, ask advice, see how it can be done. This is the last line of "The Canonization": countries, towns and courts ask the two for a pattern of their love. Waite's Hermit is the card of someone whose light others can see; in a 9-21-21 couple that light is lit for two and can be seen from the big world.
And the circle, as in Donne, ends where it began. After all the roads the couple returns to its quiet — only now this quiet is chosen, not hidden.

ul: John Donne, "The Canonization", "The Good-Morrow", "The Sun Rising", "The Anniversary", "A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning" — after H. J. C. Grierson, The Poems of John Donne, Oxford, 1912; spelling modernised.
Izaak Walton, The Life of Dr. John Donne (first edition 1640) — the secret wedding, the "Un-done" signature, Pyrford and Mitcham, the Mitcham letters, the "Valediction" given to his wife.
John Donne, Devotions upon Emergent Occasions (1624), Meditation XVII; the Russian article quotes it from the epigraph to the Russian translation of Hemingway's "For Whom the Bell Tolls".
A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911): The Hermit, The Lovers, The Moon, The World.
Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015): The Hermit, The Lovers, The Moon, The World.
Yuliana Lisovskaya, Matritsa sudby: sovmestimost (Destiny Matrix: Compatibility, 2024): the meaning of a couple's points, energies 6, 9, 18 and 21.

intro: The three cards of the tail stand in the sphere "The couple's karmic tail" and are read in order:

ul: **9, The Hermit — entry to the task.** What the couple wants together: quiet, depth, a room of their own, an unhurried pace. Everything starts from this wish, and this is also where it gets stuck: the two close off easily.
**21, The World — middle of the task.** How the couple lives the path: building a universe for two — its own language, its own philosophy, sometimes its own country on the map.

**21, The World — main task.** The main test: connecting their world to the big one. On the minus side the circle shrinks to four walls; on the plus side it widens, and people leave it and come back to it.

intro: This plot is written not only in the cards. Four hundred years ago the English poet John Donne put it into a single stanza — in order, card by card. That is where the investigation begins.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 9-21-21 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail with The Hermit at the entry and The World in both the middle and the main task. The two want quiet and shelter in each other, build a world for two, and the main test is to connect that world with the big one: friends, roads, change. It is a task for self-knowledge, not a forecast.

faq.q: Why does the couple's tail have two Worlds in a row?
faq.a: The middle and the main task are different roles. The first World shows how the couple lives the path: a universe for two. The second is the main task: that universe's relationship with the outside world. In such couples both 21s are always exact sums of the partners' points, and together they give 42 → 6 — The Lovers in the centre.

faq.q: Can 9-21-21 be a personal karmic tail?
faq.a: No. In a personal chart the middle of the tail equals the sum of the entry and the main task, and with 9 and 21 it would be a three, The Empress. A middle of 21 only appears in a couple, when it is added up from the middles of two partners.

faq.q: How can a couple tell that its tail is 9-21-21?
faq.a: Calculate compatibility from the two birth dates. The tail stands in the sphere "The couple's karmic tail": three cards — entry to the task, middle of the task and main task. For example, the dates 14.10.1975 and 05.11.1975 give exactly 9-21-21.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. The calculation gives no other couple tails made of the numbers 9, 21 and 21, so 9-21-21 cannot be confused with anything: it has only one order.

faq.q: Is the tail 9-21-21 a bad sign for a relationship?
faq.a: No. A tail does not predict events and promises nothing. It describes a task: not letting solitude for two turn into a closed circle. On the plus side the same cards make a deep, calm couple that people are drawn to.

report: The two whom love "made one another's hermitage" were promised sainthood by John Donne: the lovers of the future would pray to them. The stanza from "The Canonization" goes on — these two "did the whole world's soul contract" and drove countries, towns and courts into the glasses of their eyes, and now they are asked to beg from above a pattern of their love. Four hundred years ago Donne wrote down the tail 9-21-21 in order, card by card.

First the hermitage — The Hermit at the entry to the task: the two want to be each other's shelter. Then the whole world, shrunk to the size of a pupil — The World in the middle: the couple lives inside a universe of its own. And finally those beyond the threshold asking for a pattern — The World again, the main task: connecting their own universe to the big one.

report.h3: The quiet it all began with

report: "The Canonization" opens with a shout: "For God's sake hold your tongue, and let me love." A couple with this tail starts from the same wish — to be left alone. Friends hear about the engagement after the rings are bought. The third invitation of the month is declined, and both are glad. A conversation at dinner ends at three in the morning. Every step is taken slowly — from the first kiss to a shared key.

But the same wish can turn into resistance. The hiding place worked too well: the world moved on, and the money in their pockets was worthless. This is how a hermitage becomes a burrow — problems pile up in silence, because any hard conversation would break the quiet.

In "The Good-Morrow" love "makes one little room an everywhere". Let sea-discoverers chase new worlds: "each hath one, and is one". The two develop a language of their own, a philosophy of their own, chores split down the middle; often a literal world too — a move abroad, a life between two addresses.

Then Donne sees in the eyes of the two the two hemispheres of one globe: "My face in thine eye, thine in mine appears." A personal chart never has such a middle: The Empress, house and household, would stand there between The Hermit and The World. The couple walks the path not through a house but through a universe that neither of the two has alone.

The main task is read through what does not work. For it Donne has a funny, arrogant poem, "The Sun Rising". The lovers chase the sun out of the bedroom, call hours and days "the rags of time" and announce: **"She is all states, and all princes, I, / Nothing else is."** "This bed thy centre is, these walls, thy sphere."

This is what The World looks like when it shrinks to four walls. Friends drop away one by one. One partner's hobby becomes "not ours" and gets mocked. One re-educates the other into the shared worldview. Evenings repeat like Groundhog Day, and any novelty is met as a threat. When it gets cramped, someone slams the door, comes back and slams it again. In "The Anniversary" Donne himself names the weak spot of such a fortress: no one can betray it "except one of us two". Most often not by a loud act, but by the silence of the one who has long wanted out.

If, however, one partner forbids the other friends and family and will not let them go, that is no longer solitude but control; it calls for a counsellor or psychologist, and in danger, a local emergency number or crisis line.

report.h3: The man who did not want to be an island

report: Donne was writing about himself. In 1601 he secretly married seventeen-year-old Anne More, lost his post and went to prison, and, as his biographer tells it, signed a letter to his wife: "John Donne, Anne Donne, Un-done." Then came years of an almost hermit's life in a cramped house near London. From there he wrote to a friend: **"to be no part of any body, is as to be nothing."** The man who declared in verse that beyond the two of them "nothing else is" was, in prose, homesick for the big world. And in 1624 he wrote the sentence everyone knows: "No man is an island, entire of itself."

report.h3: A circle drawn by spreading the legs

report: Donne found the way out in "A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning", which, his biographer says, he gave to his wife before leaving for France. There the two are the legs of a pair of compasses. One sits in the centre, the other roams far; the first "leans and hearkens after it, / And grows erect, as that comes home." And the conclusion: "Thy firmness makes my circle just, / And makes me end where I begun."

**A circle only appears when the legs are apart.** Pressed together, they make a dot. A leg that runs off without a centre draws a line. Even the last line matches the numbers: the main task plus the centre lead back to the entry, 21 + 6 = 27 → 9, The World and The Lovers give The Hermit. The circle closes on the same hermitage, only now the two return to it instead of hiding in it.

In Donne the wife stands and he himself roams — that was how things were arranged in 1611. The couple's tail does not care about sex: either partner can hold the centre or take to the road, and a strong couple swaps legs. In practice this means a regular evening with an open door, a road of one's own for each without accusations of betrayal, a ritual of return, asking about the partner's world as about an unfamiliar country instead of reshaping it to the shared philosophy. Parting for such a couple is, in Donne's words, not a breach "but an expansion, / Like gold to airy thinness beat."

There is a trap in the centre too. A couple "canonized for love" is frightening to touch: every quarrel feels like sacrilege. But the pattern asked for in the stanza is alive, not an icon. In the strong version of 9-21-21 the hermitage stays a hermitage — with windows and a door. People come to such a couple on their own, to sit in the kitchen and see how it can be done.
